title: I Think Our Son Is Gay
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Homemaker Tomoko Aoyama is fairly sure her high-school son Hiroki is gay; he keeps nearly revealing it through slips of the tongue. She supports him quietly and waits for him to tell her himself, while younger son Yuri already knows and father Akiyoshi, often away for work, sometimes hurts Hiroki with outdated remarks. Short comic chapters follow family life, Hiroki's crush on classmate Daigo and his friend Asumi's feelings for him.
life_message: A family's quiet, patient acceptance lets a child become himself in his own time.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Hurtful remarks are met with patience and indirect nudges, not confrontation (ANN).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Tomoko lets Hiroki decide when to come out, within an ordinary orderly household.

Civic vs kin.evidence: The family unit is the story's center (MU Familial Love, Mother and Son).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Parents guide gently; the father's authority does not settle the question.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Traditional views on sexuality are shown as outdated (Wikipedia on the father).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Self-acceptance and tolerance are the central values.

folkways.japan: The family's indirectness (Tomoko never outs Hiroki and nudges her husband via a BL drama) reflects Japanese norms of reading the air and avoiding open confrontation at home.

delivery.evidence: ANN calls the approach like a heart-to-heart with a trusted adult; acceptance shown through family scenes rather than lectures.
delivery.note: The traditional view is carried by a loving but careless father rather than a villain; its strongest form is not argued, and the story's sympathy rests with acceptance.

winners_losers: Hiroki and his accepting mother win; the father's views are shown as hurtful and outdated, though he remains a loving parent.
to_verify: Whether the father changes his views in later volumes
